{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In [[category theory]], a '''Lawvere theory''' (named after [[United States|American]] [[mathematician]] [[William Lawvere]]) is a [[category (mathematics)|category]] that can be considered a categorical counterpart of the notion of an [[equational theory]]. Intuitively, it is a categorical generalization of algebraic structures (e.g., a group or a ring), where there exists a "generic" object and all objects are isomorphic to an integer power of <math>x</math>, representing the inputs for the <math>n</math>-ary operations on <math>x</math> (i.e., of the form <math>x^n \mapsto x</math>, starting from the fact that <math>x := x^1</math> and so <math>x \circ x := x^1 \circ x^1 := x^1x^1 := x^2</math>; trivially generalizing inductively, we get the rest of the objects) where the operations come from the algebraic structure at hand (e.g., addition and/or multiplication).

The Lawvere theory of groups has as its generic object an underlying placeholder <math>x</math> where the other objects are the inputs for <math>n</math>-ary operations from those integer powers of <math>x</math> of the form (<math>x^n</math>) back to <math>x</math>, where a model, a finite-product preserving functor, from this theory into a target category <math>C</math> such as the category of sets or topological spaces, would map the abstract theory <math>x</math> onto the category to create a concrete, "combined," group-based structure. This model would provide a set with group structure (a ''group'') or a topological space with group structure (a ''topological group''), supplying appropriate names to the generic object <math>x</math> and its mappings (<math>n</math>-ary operations) according to whatever the theory and model at play are; in the model of sets for the Lawvere theory of groups, the generic object is a group and its mappings are group operations.

==Definition==

Let <math>\aleph_0</math> be a [[skeleton (category_theory)|skeleton]] of the category '''[[FinSet]]''' of [[finite set]]s and [[function (mathematics)|function]]s. Formally, a '''Lawvere theory''' consists of a [[small category]] <math>L</math> with (strictly [[associativity|associative]]) finite [[product (category theory)|product]]s and a strict identity-on-objects [[functor (category theory)|functor]] <math>I:\aleph_0^\text{op}\rightarrow L</math> preserving finite products.

A '''model''' of a Lawvere theory in a category <math>C</math> with finite products is a finite-product preserving functor <math>M : L \rightarrow C</math>.  A '''morphism of models''' <math>h : M \rightarrow N</math> where <math>M</math> and ''<math>N</math>'' are models of ''<math>L</math>'' is a [[natural transformation]] of functors.

== Model examples ==
Some examples of models of the Lawvere theory of groups (i.e., <math>L</math> = <math>\mathbf{LawGrp}</math>):

* <math>M : L \rightarrow \mathbf{Set}</math> (<math>M</math> is a classical [[Group (mathematics)|''group'']])
* <math>M : L \rightarrow \mathbf{Top}</math> (<math>M</math> is a [[Topological group|topological ''group'']])
* <math>M : L \rightarrow \mathbf{Man}</math> (<math>M</math> is a [[Lie group|Lie ''group'']]).

Some examples of models of the Lawvere theory of rings (i.e., <math>L</math> = <math>\mathbf{LawRing}</math>):

* <math>M : L \rightarrow \mathbf{Set}</math> (<math>M</math> is a classical ''[[Ring (mathematics)|ring]]'')
* <math>M : L \rightarrow \mathbf{Top}</math> (<math>M</math> is a [[Topological ring|topological ''ring'']])
* <math>M : L \rightarrow \mathbf{Man}</math> (<math>M</math> is a [[Smooth algebra|smooth ''ring'']]).

==Category of Lawvere theories==

A '''map''' between Lawvere theories <math>(L, I)</math> and <math>(L', I')</math> is a finite-product preserving functor that commutes with <math>I</math> and <math>I'</math>. Such a map is commonly seen as an interpretation of <math>(L, I)</math> in <math>(L', I')</math>.

More formally, a map <math>K : (L, I) \rightarrow (L', I')</math>, such that <math>K \circ I = I'</math>, where <math>I(n) = x^n_{L}</math> and <math>(K \circ I)(n) = I'(n) = x^n_{L'}</math>.

Lawvere theories together with maps between them form the category <math>\mathbf{Law}</math>.

==Variations<!--'Multisorted Lawvere theory', 'Multityped Lawvere theory', 'Infinitary Lawvere theory', 'Fermat theory', and 'Finite-product theory' redirect here; boldface per WP:R#PLA-->==
Variations include '''multisorted''' (or '''multityped''') '''Lawvere theory''', '''infinitary Lawvere theory''', and '''finite-product theory'''.<ref>{{nlab|id=Lawvere+theory|title=Lawvere theory}}</ref>
